To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

47% of antibiotic use in our tertiary hospital was inappropriate and that risk factors for inappropriate antibiotic use included bone/joint infection, the absence of a microbiology result, carbapenems or macrolides and being under the supervision of the aged care and rehabilitation team.

the point‐prevalences of inappropriate antibiotic prescribing in the inpatient setting were 47% overall, with a wide variation between specialties and that inappropriate antibiotic prescribing is more likely in patients with bone/joint infections and those who were under the care of an aged care/rehab team.

the prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic prescribing was 43% and the most common reasons for inappropriate prescribing were the absence of infection (27%), discordance between clinical presentation and microbiological results (25%) and use of antibiotics outside guidelines (24%).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method for the detection of antibiotic resistance in bacteria and its application to the study of antibiotic resistance in a hospital setting.
the development of a point‐prevalent study to determine the prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic use in a tertiary hospital.
the development of an effective and sustainable antimicrobial stewardship program at our tertiary hospital and to improve antibiotic use in our hospital.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a need to improve the quality of antibiotic use in Australia.
the results of this study suggest that the use of antibiotics was inappropriate in 47% of cases, which is consistent with the findings of similar studies.
there is insufficient evidence to support the routine use of probiotics in the prevention and treatment of antibiotic-associated diarrhoea.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic use was high, with risk factors including bone/joint infections and the absence of an infection.
we have identified a significant proportion of inappropriate antibiotic use in the inpatient setting and have identified risk factors that can be used to target interventions.
the prevalence of inappropriate antibiotic use was high in this tertiary Australian hospital and that the most common reasons were the absence of infection and discordance with microbiology results.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are many reasons why patients receive antibiotics that are inappropriate and we need to be mindful of these when we are designing interventions to improve antibiotic prescribing.
there is still a significant proportion of patients who receive inappropriate antibiotics, and we have identified some key areas for intervention to help improve antibiotic use.
there is still much work to do in terms of reducing inappropriate antibiotic use.
